title: Signs in Passing
transcript: At an airport where two corridors met, passengers regularly asked a staff member which way to walk for connecting flights. A digital sign overhead already gave directions, but it alternated the arrow with weather reports and reminders about shops. Observers found that passengers usually glanced up while walking and rarely waited for the screen to change. For a week, the airport kept the arrow in the same corner of the display and let other material change around it. Staff received fewer questions about the direction of connecting flights. Questions about how long it took to reach the gates remained common, so the airport added walking times beside the arrow. In planning another display, the design team began by timing how long people actually looked at the screen.

questions.prompt: What did the airport change for the first week of the trial?
options: It reduced the brightness of the screen.
It moved the display closer to the gates.
It kept the directional arrow in a fixed corner.
It replaced weather reports with flight numbers.
questions.answer: It kept the directional arrow in a fixed corner.
questions.explanation: 试行期间，机场将方向箭头固定在屏幕同一个角落。

questions.prompt: What principle is the design team likely to apply to its next display?
options: Make essential information readable within the time passengers typically look.
Show more travel information when the corridors are busiest.
Place directions and walking times on separate screens.
Use frequent changes to encourage passengers to stop and look.
questions.answer: Make essential information readable within the time passengers typically look.
questions.explanation: 固定箭头后问路减少，团队设计新屏幕时也先测量旅客实际注视的时长。
